messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 23
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Urban Planner
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Kwame is a 23-year-old urban planner who had been proud, before the assault, of how easily he moved through the city. He spent his days visiting redevelopment sites, attending community meetings, and talking with residents about traffic, housing, and public space. The attack happened after an evening planning meeting in a neighborhood corridor where he often worked. As he was leaving, a man who smelled strongly of alcohol began arguing nearby, his voice sharp and heated. Kwame remembered noticing the smell first, then the change in the man’s face as the argument escalated. Someone threw an object—he can no longer clearly say what it was—and in the confusion the man turned on him. What remains with Kwame is not a coherent story he can easily tell but a set of frozen images: the glint of something moving through the air, the man’s angry expression, the alcoholic sourness on his breath, his own sense that events were already in motion and he could not stop what came next. When he tries to describe the assault in detail, he loses words. He knows it happened; he can point to fragments of it with painful certainty, but if he stays with the memory for more than a moment he becomes flooded and has to stop speaking.

In the weeks afterward, the city that had once felt like his field of work began to feel volatile and unreadable. At planning meetings, if residents disagreed with one another and someone’s tone sharpened—even calmly—Kwame’s body reacted before he could reason with it. A chair scraping, a binder dropped on a table, a quick gesture in his peripheral vision would make him jolt hard enough to embarrass him. He started watching hands, shoulders, and sudden movement around him, as though danger might announce itself in a twitch. Colleagues would tell him that a meeting was under control or that a site visit was perfectly safe, but he found he could not take that in. Other people’s reassurance seemed flimsy to him. He had come to believe that safety was exactly the sort of thing people say right before something goes wrong.

What frightened him almost as much as the memories was what they seemed to mean about him. He dwelled on what he should have done differently that night: whether he should have left earlier, whether he should have avoided the argument, whether he had missed some obvious sign. These thoughts circled for hours, often late at night, and never arrived anywhere. He also became convinced that the people and systems that were supposed to protect him had failed. He had expected that public space, event security, and the basic structures around civic work would count for something; after the assault, that assumption felt naïve. More and more, he was certain that bad things could happen without warning and that when they did, he would not be able to stop them. Even minor upsets began to feel like proof that he could no longer cope. If a conversation became tense, or a project hit an obstacle, he felt internally brittle, as though the smallest disturbance might push him past what he could manage.

Over the following months, Kwame changed his routines in ways that looked practical from the outside but steadily narrowed his life. He began avoiding any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation. At work, that meant speaking less in public meetings, declining to facilitate contentious sessions, and asking coworkers to take the lead when residents were upset about zoning or construction. He started choosing site visits that seemed quieter and avoiding community events where tempers sometimes flared. Being single, he had once relied on friends and colleagues for much of his social life, but he also pulled back from them, especially if getting together meant bars, parties, or anywhere he might catch the smell of alcohol. If someone nearby had been drinking, his body tightened immediately and his attention locked onto exits, gestures, and distance.

At night, he found another way to get out of himself. He started gambling online, telling himself it was just a distraction, then noticing he sought the jolt of it—the brief, sharp excitement that cut across the heaviness and agitation. It gave him something immediate to focus on other than the pictures in his head. Still, afterward he often felt ashamed and more critical of himself, which fed the same familiar loop of thinking about what he had done wrong.

By the time he came for help, the pattern had begun to affect his work visibly. He was still showing up, still trying to function as an urban planner, but meetings that once fit him well now felt like exposure to something he could not control. What finally brought him in was a recent incident in which a colleague, frustrated but not threatening, slapped a rolled set of plans onto a conference table. Kwame jerked back so abruptly that the room fell silent. He left before the meeting ended and later sat in his car unable to explain, even to himself, why his chest was pounding so hard. He said he was tired of living as if any sudden movement or flash of anger could become another assault. At the same time, he was afraid that talking about what happened would overwhelm him completely, and afraid that the larger truth might be that no place is really safe and no one meant to protect him ever truly did.
